notes.gdp_per_capita: Eurostat says this series is mainly for comparing countries with each other, not for comparing a country with its own past.
notes.pisa_math: PISA mathematics, 2003 to 2022. Luxembourg has no 2022 value. The OECD average is shown because PISA has no EU27 average. Countries outside Europe appear only when a PISA indicator is selected.
notes.pisa_reading: PISA reading, 2000 to 2022. The OECD average for 2003 to 2009 is calculated from the OECD countries in the data, and is within about 3 points of the official average where that can be checked; there is no OECD average for 2000. Countries outside Europe appear only when a PISA indicator is selected.
notes.pisa_science: PISA science, 2006 to 2022. The OECD average for 2006 and 2009 is calculated from the OECD countries in the data, and is within about 3 points of the official average where that can be checked. Countries outside Europe appear only when a PISA indicator is selected.
notes.life_expectancy: Life expectancy at birth, annual, total population, from Eurostat.
notes.gini: Gini coefficient on a 0–100 scale. Lower means more equal. Rank 1 is the most equal country.
notes.median_income_pps: Median equivalised net income in purchasing power standard (PPS), so countries compare on equal terms.
notes.median_income_eur: Median equivalised net income in euro. Prices differ between countries, so PPS is better for comparing living standards.
notes.inflation: Ranked by distance from 2%, the usual central bank target: the country closest to 2% ranks first.

explain.unemployment: The share of the labour force that is unemployed. The labour force is everyone aged 15 to 74 who either has a job or is actively looking for one. People who are not looking for work, such as most students and retirees, are not part of the labour force and are not counted. An unemployment rate of 8% means that 8 in every 100 people in the labour force are without work and looking for it. Lower is better.
explain.inflation: The annual change in consumer prices, measured with the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP). It compares the average price of a typical basket of goods and services, such as food, housing, energy and transport, with the previous year. At 2%, a basket that cost €100 last year costs €102 this year. A negative value means prices fell. The European Central Bank and most other European central banks aim for inflation of about 2%, so countries are ranked by how close they are to 2%.
explain.gdp_per_capita: Gross domestic product (GDP) per person in purchasing power standards (PPS), as an index where the EU average is 100. GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. PPS removes differences in price levels between countries, so the figures compare real volumes. A value of 120 means 20% above the EU average. Large multinational companies and cross-border commuters can raise GDP, so it does not always reflect household incomes; median income is a better guide to those. Eurostat recommends this index for comparing countries, not for tracking one country over time. Higher is better.
explain.at_risk_of_poverty: The share of people whose equivalised disposable income is below 60% of the national median. Disposable income is income after taxes and social transfers; equivalised means it is adjusted for household size. The threshold is set separately for each country, so this is a measure of relative poverty: it shows how many people fall well below the typical income in their own country, not whether they can afford a fixed standard of living. Lower is better.
explain.median_income_pps: The median equivalised disposable income per year, in purchasing power standards (PPS). The median is the middle value: half the population has a higher income and half a lower one. Disposable income is what remains after taxes and social transfers. Equivalised means household income is adjusted for household size and composition, so that a single person and a family of four can be compared; the family needs more income, but not four times as much. PPS removes differences in price levels between countries. Higher is better.
explain.median_income_eur: The median equivalised disposable income per year, in euros, without adjusting for price levels. It shows the actual amounts of money. Price levels vary widely across Europe, so the PPS version is better for comparing living standards. Higher is better.
explain.gini: The Gini coefficient measures how evenly income is distributed, on a scale from 0 to 100. A value of 0 would mean everyone has the same income; 100 would mean one person receives all of it. It is calculated from equivalised disposable income. Among the countries here, recent values range from about 22 (Slovakia) to about 38 (Bulgaria). It measures inequality only, not the overall level of income. Lower means more equal, and rank 1 is the most equal country.
explain.life_expectancy: The average number of years a newborn would live if the death rates of their year of birth stayed the same throughout their life. It summarises that year's mortality and is not a forecast. It reflects health care, living conditions, lifestyle and accident rates, among other things. In Finland it was 82.2 years in 2024. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_math: The OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) tests 15-year-olds, normally every three years. The most recent results in this data are from 2022. The mathematics test measures how well students can apply mathematics to real-world problems. Scores are country averages on a scale set so that the OECD average was 500 in 2003, when mathematics was first the main subject. In the EU in 2022, scores ranged from 417 (Bulgaria) to 510 (Estonia). Differences of a few points are usually within the margin of error. PISA has no EU average, so the OECD average is shown instead. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_reading: The PISA reading test measures how well students can understand, use, evaluate and reflect on written texts, such as articles, instructions and online messages. The scale was set so that the OECD average was 500 in 2000. As with mathematics, differences of a few points are usually within the margin of error, and the OECD average is shown for comparison. Higher is better.
explain.pisa_science: The PISA science test measures how well students can explain phenomena scientifically, evaluate and design scientific enquiry, and interpret data and evidence. The scale was set so that the OECD average was 500 in 2006; earlier results are not directly comparable and are not shown. Differences of a few points are usually within the margin of error, and the OECD average is shown for comparison. Higher is better.
